'''Aklilu Lemma''' ({{Langx |am|አክሊሉ ለማ}}; 18 September 1935{{spaced en dash}}5 April 1997) was an Ethiopian [[pathologist]].<ref name=":0222">{{cite encyclopedia|year=2003|title=Aklilu Lemma|encyclopedia=Encyclopaedia Aethiopica|publisher=Harrassowitz Verlag|location=Wiesbaden|last=Bekele|first=Shiferaw|volume=1|pages=172}}</ref> In 1989, he was awarded the [[Right Livelihood Award]] "for discovering and campaigning relentlessly for an affordable preventative against [[bilharzia]]."<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://rightlivelihood.org/the-change-makers/find-a-laureate/aklilu-lemma/|title=Aklilu Lemma|website=The Right Livelihood Award|language=en-US|access-date=2025-04-16}}</ref>  He made his most important scientific discovery very early in his career in 1964 when he discovered a natural environmental control agent for schistosomiasis, also known as snail fever or bilharzia. He found that berries from the [[endod]] plant, which are commonly used to make soap and shampoos in many parts of Africa, are a potent, inexpensive and safe molluscicide, to prevent the spread of the parasitic worm via infected aquatic snails. This discovery made the plant an object of scientific research in many parts of the world. 

== Education==
Lemma was educated at [[Addis Ababa University|Addis Ababa University College]], [[Northwestern University]], [[University of Wisconsin Madison]]<ref>{{cite book|chapter-url=https://www.dbnl.org/tekst/oltm003ongr02_01/oltm003ongr02_01_0027.php|chapter=27. Aklilu Lemma|pages=191-194|title=On Growth II|year=1975|last=Oltmans|first=Willem L.|publisher=Capricorn Books/G.P. Putnam's Sons|location=New York|oclc=1531766|access-date=2025-04-16|via=De Digitale Bibliotheek voor de Nederlandse Letteren}}</ref> and at [[Johns Hopkins University]] in the U.S.<ref name=":1"/> where he obtained his [[D.Sc.]] in 1964. His [[dissertation]] was on sandfly-borne [[leishmaniasis]].{{citation needed|date=April 2025}}

==Career==
Following his doctorate, Lemma returned to his home country, Ethiopia, where he obtained a position at the then [[Haile Selassie I University]]. He founded the Institute of Pathobiology, now known as the Aklilu Lemma Institute of Pathobiology,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aau.edu.et/alipb/|title=Aklilu Lemma Institute of Pathobiology {{!}} Seek Wisdom, Elevate your Intellect and Serve Humanity|website=www.aau.edu.et|access-date=2019-02-15|archive-date=2023-12-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231212164825/http://www.aau.edu.et/alipb/|url-status=dead}}</ref> and taught there until 1976, when he left it for a job in the [[United Nations]]. He served the UN in many capacities as a scientist, became the Deputy Director of [[UNICEF]]'s International Child Development Centre, now known as UNICEF's Innocenti Research Centre<ref name=":1" /> and finally obtained a position in his [[alma mater]], [[Johns Hopkins University]].

He made his most important scientific discovery very early in his career, in 1964, when he discovered a natural environmental preventive agent against [[schistosomiasis]],<ref name=":1"/> also known as snail fever disease or bilharzia, a debilitating disease caused by parasitic worms of genus ''[[Schistosoma]]'' spread by [[freshwater snail]]s. He found that berries from the ''[[Phytolacca dodecandra|endod]]'' plant, which is commonly used to make soap and shampoos in many parts of Africa, is a potent, inexpensive and safe [[molluscicide]], to prevent the spread of parasitic worms by reducing host snail populations.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rightlivelihoodaward.org/speech/acceptance-speech-aklilu-lemma/|title=Acceptance speech - Aklilu Lemma|website=The Right Livelihood Award|access-date=2019-02-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lemma|first=Aklilu|date=1970|title=Laboratory and Field Evaluation of the Molluscicidal Properties of Phytolacca dodecandra|journal=Bulletin of the World Health Organization|volume=42|issue=4|pages=597–612|issn=0042-9686|pmc=2427471|pmid=5310955}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mazengia|first1=B.|last2=Duncan|first2=J.|last3=Lemma|first3=A.|last4=Goll|first4=P. H.|date=September 1983|title=Control of schistosomiasis in Adwa, Ethiopia, using the plant molluscicide endod (Phytolacca dodecandra).|journal=Tropenmedizin und Parasitologie|volume=34|issue=3|pages=177–183|issn=0303-4208|pmid=6636299}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lemma|first1=Aklilu|last2=Brody|first2=Gerald|last3=Newell|first3=Gordon W.|last4=Parkhurst|first4=R. M.|last5=Skinner|first5=W. A.|date=1972|title=Studies on the Molluscicidal Properties of Endod (Phytolacca dodecandra): I. Increased Potency with Butanol Extraction|journal=The Journal of Parasitology|volume=58|issue=1|pages=104–107|doi=10.2307/3278251|issn=0022-3395|jstor=3278251|pmid=5062455 |doi-access=free}}</ref> This discovery made the plant an object of scientific research in many parts of the world. Lemma himself was at the forefront of this research. His work acquired an international reputation, which in turn led to various awards, including [[honorary doctorate]] degrees.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Aklilu Lemma International Memorial Symposium Proceedings, September 18-19, 1997|year=1997|location=Addis Ababa}}</ref> The most prestigious award was the one he won together with his research associate, Dr. [[Legesse Wolde-Yohannes]] in November 1989 – the [[Right Livelihood Award]] of [[Sweden]], commonly referred to as the Alternative Nobel Prize.<ref>{{cite web|title=Aklilu Lemma (Ethiopia) |url=http://www.rightlivelihood.org/lemma.html |publisher=Right Livelihood Award |access-date=19 February 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130925080343/http://www.rightlivelihood.org/lemma.html |archive-date=25 September 2013 }}</ref>

He died in the United States on 5 April 1997 and was buried in Ethiopia, on 13 April.<ref name=":0" />

== Awards and distinctions ==
* Right Livelihood Award (1989)
